newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries close higher, optimism persists.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries close higher, optimism persists.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed higher in active trade, boosted by fresh economic data suggesting the economy is slowing with no signs of inflation, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up 14/32 at 100-27/32. Its yield slipped to 6.44 percent, against 6.47 percent at Monday's close.

The rally was triggered by the release early in the session of a sharp 5.1 percent drop in housing starts in October to a 1.366 million annual rate. The indicator fell a revised 6.1 percent in September.
"Housing starts came in very nicely ... I think it's going to be relatively supportive to the market," said Jerry Zukowski, money market economist at PaineWebber Inc.
"Looking ahead, it doesn't look like there is too much that is going to send the market back. We're in pretty firm shape fundamentally," he added.
Analysts said the market held firm despite a somewhat disppointing Treasury two-year note auction, which met lighter-than-expected demand and sold at a higher-than-forecast yield.
"The auction went a little weaker than most had anticipated," said John Spinello, managing director of government securities at Merrill Lynch.
Pundits said the slack demand took place because Wall Street's underwriting community did not participate in the auction in a strong degree.
"The auction wasn't as well received and as easily underwritten as people thought, but (the results) haven't had a real significant effect on the market," Spinello said.
Treasuries trimmed some gains after the auction, but recovered most of the lost ground by the end of the day.

The two-year note was sold at a yield of 5.662 percent, awarding 29 percent of bids at high. The bid-to-cover ratio was below expectations at 2.11, with non-competitive bids accounting for $928 million.
So after Tuesday's auction, what can one expect for the five-year note sale on Wednesday?
"I think given that hesitancy of the underwriting of two-year notes you might get a little bit of better concession," said the head of the Treasury desk at a major U.S. investment bank.
"But it's still a little dangerous. Perhaps a little more caution will be taken tomorrow," he added.
The Treasury will sell $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday. Bidding deadline for the sale is 1300 EST/1800 GMT.
Analysts said flows were mostly broad-based. Analysts said professional players rushed back to the market to cover shorts after the release of the housing data sparked a new rally.
Traders noted some swap operations between Treasuries and Eurodollar deposits. They also said there was talk of some foreign central bank buying earlier in the day.
"Technically it doesn't look like foreign buying will necessarily be drying up. That's been the force behind this rally. We don't expect that to disappear soon," the head trader said.
Although the trading session was considered active, analysts said most of the volume was concentrated on the long end of the market.
Traded volume across the yield curve as measured by GovPX was around $70 billion by late afternoon on Tuesday, the lightest for a two-year auction day in 1996.

However, coupon trading was 33.5 percent above the daily average for Tuesday and bond traded volume rose near 25 percent. "The day was below average in terms of total volume, but the long end was above average," said Maureen Mooney, senior fixed-income specialist at GovPX.
GovPX publishes real-time Treasury prices and volume from five of the six intra-dealer brokers, representing 65 percent of the intra-dealers trades.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed unchanged at 5.03 percent. The six-month bill rate was flat at 5.06 percent.
